name: Facial ratios measurement

lead: Facial ratios measurement means placing landmarks on a front or side photo, calculating proportions such as facial width-to-height, the midface ratio or the lower-third share of face height, and comparing them to commonly quoted targets. The payoff is a concrete map of which areas (jaw, midface, chin, forehead) differ most from the target, which people use to choose what to improve.

Aesthetic clinicians also assess proportions when planning treatments, and researchers have long studied symmetry and averageness in attractiveness. The specific target numbers on forums are compiled by community members rather than from a single standard.

paras: People take a straight-on, evenly lit photo at a consistent distance, mark landmarks (pupils, nasion, subnasale, chin, cheekbones) and divide one measurement by another. Many use a longer lens or greater distance to reduce perspective distortion, and compare results against ratio lists posted on forums.

The main risk is measurement error: wide-angle lenses, head tilt and expression shift the numbers. Forum lists differ from one another and note that ideals depend on ethnicity and phenotype, so users are comparing to a loose reference rather than a clinical standard.

angle.text: Measuring turns a general impression into numbers, which people use to decide where to focus: a long lower third might prompt hair or beard choices, a short midface a different haircut or facial surgery consult. The measurement itself changes nothing; it guides the choices that do.

lead: Facial ratios measurement is the practice of measuring distances between facial landmarks on photographs and expressing them as ratios, then comparing them with target proportions. In looksmaxxing communities it is a self-assessment step: the ratios show which features sit closest to or furthest from the ideal being aimed for, and so where improvements (grooming, hair, fat loss, orthodontics, fillers or surgery) might change overall balance.

Lists posted on looksmax.org include a facial width-to-height ratio of roughly 1.8 or higher, a midface ratio of about 1.0 to 1.1, a mouth-to-nose width ratio of 1.5 to 1.62, a chin-to-philtrum ratio of 2.0 to 2.25, and a lower-to-full-face ratio of about 0.62 or more [1][2]. Posters note that the right values depend on ethnicity and phenotype [3].

Clinicians also consider proportions when planning jawline and perioral treatments, noting that men and women have different ideal facial ratios [4]. Research on attractiveness has examined symmetry and averageness, with symmetric faces generally rated as more attractive, though findings are correlational and perfect symmetry can look unnatural [5].

paras: A typical forum thread describes the measurements: the facial width-to-height ratio divides bizygomatic width by the height from the brow to the upper lip; the midface ratio divides the distance between the pupils by the nasion-to-upper-lip height, with 1:1 treated as the aim; the lower-to-full-face ratio divides nasion-to-chin height by the full face height [2]. A parallel thread gives a mouth-to-nose width ratio, a lower-to-upper-lip ratio of 1.62, a chin-to-philtrum ratio and a forehead height of three fingers [1].

Replies in these threads disagree on definitions, for instance on which eyebrow point to use for the width-to-height ratio, and on the ideal midface ratio, with one poster preferring about 1.02 and saying a slightly compact midface beats a slightly long one [1][2].

Community threads discuss measurement tools and photo conditions, including one poster's purchase of a 200 mm lens DSLR to avoid lens distortion in photos [6]. The concern is that short focal lengths at close range exaggerate the central face.

A 2021 review of jawline and perioral rejuvenation with neuromodulators and hyaluronic acid fillers states that men and women have different aging processes and ideal facial ratios that must be considered in treatment planning [4].

No studies found testing whether measuring one's own facial ratios improves outcomes. Related research on facial symmetry has found that symmetrical faces tend to be rated as more attractive and healthier-looking, with some experiments finding that averageness and symmetry contribute independently; the findings are correlational [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, ratio threads circulate lists of target values and measurement diagrams, and members debate their definitions [1][2].
